title: ser vs estar
tagline: Both mean 'to be' — but ser is identity, estar is state. The rule about permanent vs temporary will get you in trouble.

sides.core: Ser encodes what something fundamentally is — identity, category, origin, material.

examples.note: His personality. Swap to está and he's just bored right now — totally different verdict.

examples.es: La boda es en la iglesia.
examples.en: The wedding is at the church.
examples.note: Location of an event uses ser, not estar. Catches everyone out.
Appearance as identity. But 'está muy guapa hoy' means she looks great today — she made an effort.

sides.core: Estar encodes current state — how something is right now, not what it is.

examples.note: Death is permanent but it's still a state the body is in. 'Es muerto' doesn't exist.
Quality you're experiencing right now. 'Es bueno' is a general verdict; 'está bueno' is tasting it.
Versus 'es listo' = he's clever. Same adjective, completely different meaning depending on verb.

tricky: Adjectives that flip meaning: listo (clever/ready), malo (bad/sick), bueno (good/tasty), vivo (sharp/alive), seguro (safe/certain).

title: fue vs era
tagline: Both are past tense of ser — fue is a completed snapshot, era is the background scenery.

title: por vs para
tagline: Para points forward to a goal or recipient. Por looks back at cause, exchange, or movement through.

title: saber vs conocer
tagline: Saber is knowing facts and skills. Conocer is familiarity through experience — people, places, things you've encountered.

title: salir vs quedar
tagline: Quedar is making the plan to meet. Salir is the activity of going out. You can have one without the other.

title: llevar vs hacer (time)
tagline: Both express how long something has been going on — but they're built differently and can't be swapped.

title: pedir vs preguntar
tagline: Preguntar is asking a question. Pedir is asking for something — a request, an order, a demand.

title: poder vs saber (can)
tagline: Both translate as 'can' — but poder is physical ability or permission, saber is knowing how.

title: deber vs tener que
tagline: Both mean 'must' or 'have to' — deber is moral obligation, tener que is practical necessity.

title: ir vs venir
tagline: Spanish anchors movement to where the speaker is right now — the opposite of English more often than you'd think.

title: traer vs llevar
tagline: Like ir/venir but for objects — llevar is taking something away, traer is bringing it here.

title: querer vs amar
tagline: Both mean 'to love' — but querer is the everyday word for love and wanting, amar is deeper and more formal.

title: mirar vs ver
tagline: Mirar is looking (actively directing your gaze). Ver is seeing (the result — what registers in your eyes).

title: escuchar vs oír
tagline: Escuchar is listening (active). Oír is hearing (passive — sound entering your ears whether you want it or not).

title: acordarse vs recordar
tagline: Both mean 'to remember' — acordarse is reflexive and personal, recordar can also mean to remind.

title: sentir vs sentirse
tagline: Sentir is feeling or sensing something external. Sentirse is how you feel inside — your personal emotional state.

title: pensar vs creer
tagline: Both translate as 'to think' — pensar is active thinking or planning, creer is holding a belief.

title: gastar vs pasar (spend)
tagline: Both translate 'to spend' in English — gastar is spending money, pasar is spending time.

title: hablar vs decir
tagline: Hablar is talking (the activity). Decir is saying or telling (the content of what's communicated).

title: encontrar vs buscar
tagline: Buscar is the searching. Encontrar is the finding. One is the journey, one is the result.

title: perder vs faltar
tagline: Perder is losing something. Faltar is something being missing or absent — the gap itself.

title: tocar vs jugar
tagline: Both can relate to playing — jugar is playing games/sports, tocar is playing instruments and also 'touching.'

title: volver vs regresar
tagline: Both mean 'to return' — volver is universal Spanish, regresar is more Latin American and slightly more formal.

title: dejar vs salir (leave)
tagline: English 'leave' covers both — dejar is leaving something/someone behind, salir is leaving a place.

title: ser vs parecer
tagline: Ser states what something is. Parecer hedges — it seems, it looks like, you have an impression.

title: haber
tagline: The invisible backbone of Spanish — auxiliary 'have' for perfect tenses AND the existence word 'hay'. Two completely different jobs, one verb.

title: tener
tagline: Tener means 'to have' — but Spanish uses it where English says 'to be', making a whole class of sentences feel backwards.

title: hacer
tagline: Hacer means make and do — but it also does weather, time expressions, and causatives. One of the most overloaded verbs in Spanish.

title: dar
tagline: Dar means 'to give' — but it powers dozens of expressions where English uses completely different verbs.

title: poner
tagline: Poner is 'to put' — but it also sets tables, turns things on, gives names, and becomes ponerse for a whole world of change-of-state expressions.

title: gustar
tagline: Gustar doesn't mean 'to like' — it means 'to please.' The thing you like is the subject. The sentence runs in reverse.

title: tomar
tagline: Tomar is 'to take' in its broadest sense — drink, eat, catch transport, make decisions. Common in Latin America; coger fills many of the same roles in Spain.

title: coger
tagline: In Spain: totally normal — grab, take, catch. In most of Latin America: an obscenity. The single most regionally dangerous verb in Spanish.

title: entrar
tagline: To enter — sounds simple, but the preposition after it (en vs a) divides Spain and Latin America, and it often replaces 'go in' in ways English doesn't.

title: subir vs bajar
tagline: Up vs down — but also upload vs download, turn up vs turn down, get on vs get off. One axis, many contexts.

title: tirar vs sacar
tagline: Tirar is throw/pull/bin. Sacar is take out/get/produce. Both get confused with each other and with other verbs.

title: echar
tagline: Echar might be the most surprisingly versatile verb in Spanish — it means throw, pour, fire, miss someone, and powers a huge number of fixed expressions.

title: caer
tagline: Caer is 'to fall' — but in Spanish it also expresses how you feel about people, whether things suit you, and moments of realisation.

title: sentar vs sentarse
tagline: Sentarse is 'to sit down' — reflexive, which learners often drop. But sentar (without reflexive) means 'to suit' or 'to agree with' you physically.

title: seguir
tagline: Seguir means to follow AND to continue — and the structure 'seguir + gerund' is one of the most useful in Spanish.

title: esperar
tagline: Esperar covers both 'to wait' and 'to hope' — two very different things in English, handled by one verb in Spanish.

title: conseguir
tagline: Conseguir means to get, achieve, or manage to do something — not to 'follow' (that's confusing it with seguir). One of the most useful verbs learners underuse.

title: crear vs creer
tagline: One letter apart, completely different meanings — crear is to create, creer is to believe. Constantly confused in writing and sometimes in speech.

title: quedar vs quedarse
tagline: Quedar is what's left or how something fits. Quedarse is staying put. One letter pair, two different ideas.

title: volverse vs hacerse (become)
tagline: Both mean 'become' but for different kinds of change. Hacerse is chosen or earned. Volverse is a deep change that happens to you.

title: dejar de vs parar
tagline: Both mean 'stop' but dejar de quits a habit or activity for good, parar halts something physically or temporarily.

title: acabar vs terminar
tagline: Both mean 'finish' and are often interchangeable — but acabar also means 'just did' and 'run out of', and terminar is the cleaner choice for completing a task.

title: soler vs acostumbrarse
tagline: Soler means 'to usually do'. Acostumbrarse means 'to get used to'. English uses 'used to' for both ideas and learners tangle them.

title: darse cuenta vs realizar
tagline: 'Realize' in English means to notice, but realizar in Spanish means to carry out. A classic false friend.

title: asistir vs atender
tagline: 'Assist' is a trap. Asistir means to attend an event; atender means to serve someone or pay attention.

title: soportar vs apoyar
tagline: 'Support' splits in two. Soportar is to bear or put up with. Apoyar is to back someone or lean something on a surface.

title: introducir vs presentar
tagline: 'Introduce' someone is presentar. Introducir is to insert or bring in something new.

title: pretender vs fingir
tagline: False friend alert. 'Pretend' in English is fingir. Pretender means to intend or aim to do something.

title: avergonzado vs embarazada
tagline: The most embarrassing false friend. 'Estoy embarazada' is not 'I'm embarrassed' — it means 'I'm pregnant'.

title: conducir vs manejar
tagline: Both mean 'to drive', split by region. Conducir in Spain, manejar across Latin America — and manejar means 'handle' in Spain.

title: probar vs intentar
tagline: 'Try' covers two ideas. Probar is to test or taste. Intentar is to attempt.

title: mover vs mudarse
tagline: 'Move' in English has two meanings. Mover is to shift something. Mudarse is to move house.

title: aprender vs enseñar
tagline: Learn vs teach — and enseñar also means 'show'. Mixing them up is one of the few errors that flips who's doing what.

title: dar vs regalar
tagline: Dar is general giving. Regalar is giving a gift — no payment, no reason beyond kindness or celebration.

title: prestar vs pedir prestado
tagline: English 'borrow' and 'lend' are two verbs. Spanish has prestar for lending and needs a whole phrase, pedir prestado, to borrow.

title: llamar vs llamarse
tagline: Llamar is to call someone or to name something. Llamarse is to be named. The reflexive 'se' matters.

title: levantar vs levantarse
tagline: Levantar is lifting something. Levantarse is getting up yourself. The reflexive marks who is doing the rising.

title: ir vs irse
tagline: Ir is going toward a place. Irse is leaving, departing from where you are.

title: dormir vs dormirse
tagline: Dormir is the state of sleeping. Dormirse is the moment of falling asleep.

title: estar de acuerdo vs acordar
tagline: 'Agree' needs two Spanish forms. Estar de acuerdo is to share an opinion. Acordar is to settle a decision together.

title: hacer falta vs necesitar
tagline: Both express need. Necesitar puts you as the subject. Hacer falta works like gustar — the thing needed is the subject.

title: importar vs interesar
tagline: Both follow the gustar pattern. Importar is 'to matter' or 'to mind'. Interesar is 'to be interested in'. And importar also means 'import'.

title: funcionar vs trabajar
tagline: In English a machine 'works' as well as a person. In Spanish, machines funcionan and people trabajan.

title: cumplir
tagline: Cumplir means to fulfil — which covers birthdays, promises, rules and sentences. English uses a different verb for each.

title: llegar vs alcanzar
tagline: Llegar is arriving. Alcanzar is reaching — by stretching, catching up, or achieving.

title: quitar vs quitarse
tagline: Quitar is taking something away. Quitarse is taking off your own clothes or stepping aside. The reflexive points back at you.

title: llevar vs vestirse (wear)
tagline: English 'wear' has no single Spanish match. Llevar is the state of wearing, vestirse is the process of dressing, and ponerse is the act of putting on.

title: ganar vs ganarse
tagline: Ganar is to win or earn. Ganarse is to earn something through your own effort — the reflexive stresses that you've deserved it.

title: soñar
tagline: Soñar con is the key phrase. You dream 'with' something in Spanish, both when sleeping and when aspiring.

title: olvidar vs olvidarse
tagline: Olvidar is to forget something. Olvidarse de is the same thing in a more personal way — and 'se me olvidó' is the structure that makes it accidental.

title: notar vs fijarse
tagline: Notar is to notice or sense passively. Fijarse is to pay attention on purpose — to look carefully.

title: preocupar vs preocuparse
tagline: Preocupar means 'to worry someone' — gustar-style. Preocuparse means 'to worry yourself'. Both are common and easy to mix up.

title: resultar
tagline: Resultar means 'to turn out' — but also fills gaps where Spanish avoids ser or tener, especially with 'me resulta'.

title: sobrar vs bastar
tagline: Sobrar means there's too much or some left over. Bastar means that's enough. Neighbours on the same scale.

title: costar vs valer
tagline: Both express price. Costar is what you pay. Valer is what something is worth. Valer also means 'to be okay'.

title: durar vs tardar
tagline: Both measure time. Durar is how long something lasts. Tardar is how long it takes to get done or arrive.

title: pagar vs cobrar
tagline: Pagar is handing over money. Cobrar is receiving it — as a wage, a fee or a bill.

title: mandar vs enviar
tagline: Both mean 'to send'. Enviar is neutral and a touch formal; mandar is common in speech and also means 'to order'.

title: casarse
tagline: Casarse con — you marry 'with' someone in Spanish. The preposition and the reflexive are both non-negotiable.

title: despedir vs despedirse
tagline: Despedir is to fire someone or see them off. Despedirse is to say goodbye yourself.

title: morir vs matar
tagline: Morir is to die. Matar is to kill. The reflexive forms morirse and matarse change the tone completely.

title: oler vs saber a
tagline: Oler is smell and saber a is taste — but saber is also 'to know'. The preposition 'a' signals flavour.

title: cerrar vs apagar
tagline: English 'turn off' has two Spanish forms. Cerrar closes taps, doors, accounts. Apagar switches off lights, devices, flames.

title: arreglar vs arreglarse
tagline: Arreglar is fixing, tidying or sorting something. Arreglarse is getting ready and managing — the reflexive brings it back to you.

title: pegar
tagline: Pegar means to hit, to stick and to match — three unrelated meanings, plus a family of 'give a shout/jump' expressions.

title: meter vs poner
tagline: Poner places something on a surface. Meter puts something inside. 'Put' needs two verbs in Spanish.

title: andar vs caminar
tagline: Both mean 'to walk'. Caminar is the neutral verb. Andar is looser and often means 'to be' or 'to go about'.

title: comprender vs entender
tagline: Both mean 'to understand'. Entender is the everyday verb. Comprender suggests deeper or empathetic understanding — and also means 'to include'.

title: discutir vs comentar
tagline: 'Discuss' is a false friend. Discutir means to argue. Comentar is to talk through, remark on or mention.

title: tratar vs tratarse
tagline: Tratar de is to try. Tratar a is to treat someone. Tratarse de is 'it's about'. Three prepositions, three meanings.

title: dedicar vs dedicarse
tagline: Dedicar is to devote or dedicate something. Dedicarse a is to do for a living — the question '¿a qué te dedicas?' is everywhere.

title: hay que vs tener que
tagline: Both express obligation. Hay que is impersonal — 'one has to'. Tener que is personal and names who must do it.

title: aprobar vs suspender
tagline: English 'pass' an exam is aprobar, not pasar. And suspender is to fail — but also to suspend and cancel.

title: caber
tagline: Caber means 'to fit inside'. It's irregular, little-used by learners, and has several idioms with a surprising reach.

title: disfrutar vs gozar
tagline: Both mean 'to enjoy'. Disfrutar is the everyday word. Gozar is more formal and often means to possess a benefit, like good health.
